c.tagline: Bangladesh's tea-garden gateway of saintly shrines, wetlands and diaspora ties to Britain.

taxi.fareNote: Metered taxis are rare; the green CNG auto-rickshaws are the main hired option and fares must be negotiated up front. App rides (Uber, Pathao) have a limited presence in Sylhet but give upfront pricing when available.

emergency.note: 999 is Bangladesh's free 24/7 national emergency number connecting to police, fire, and ambulance; English-speaking operators are available.

hood_landmark.Dargah Gate (Shah Jalal): Shrine of Hazrat Shah Jalal, Sylhet

avoid.reason: Steer clear of political rallies and hartal (strike) crowds, which can turn volatile, and watch bags in busy bazaars like Zinda Bazar.

hood_desc: Sylhet's bustling commercial core and busiest shopping strip, packed with markets, restaurants, banks and the city's best mid-range and upscale hotels; the natural first-timer base with everything walkable.

A major transport crossroads just north of the center with shopping centres, cheap eateries and easy connections toward the airport and Lakkatura tea garden; convenient and budget-friendly, if busy and traffic-heavy.

The spiritual heart of the city around the revered shrine (dargah) of the 14th-century saint Hazrat Shah Jalal, drawing pilgrims day and night amid its pond of holy catfish; atmospheric and central, best for visitors focused on the shrines.

A planned, leafy upscale residential district on the southern edge of the city, just north of the Surma River, with wide blocks, walled villas, cafes and quieter mid-to-high-end hotels; suits travelers wanting calm and comfort away from the downtown crush.

The green corridor running north toward Osmani airport, dotted with resorts, the Grand Sylhet hotel and tea-estate scenery; good for a resort-style stay and quick airport access, though a taxi ride from downtown life.

water.note: Drink bottled or filtered water only.

transit.hours: Buses, CNG auto-rickshaws and cycle-rickshaws run from early morning to mid-evening; after dark, CNGs and the limited ride apps are the main option.
transit.note: Sylhet has no metro or urban rail; getting around means green CNG auto-rickshaws, cycle-rickshaws, shared human-haulers (leguna) and local buses, with Bangladesh Railway and intercity coaches linking the city to Dhaka and beyond.
transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash directly to the driver; CNG and rickshaw fares are negotiated up front, while local bus fares are a low flat rate. There is no transit card, and app rides (Uber, Pathao) give upfront pricing where available.

train: Sylhet Railway Station (Bangladesh Railway) - intercity trains to Dhaka and Chittagong

transit.m: CNG auto-rickshaw to Zindabazar/city center (negotiate fare, ~25-35 min)
Uber/Pathao ride to city center where available (~25 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up or 5-10% is appreciated at upscale restaurants and hotels; not expected for CNGs, rickshaws or local buses, though small change is welcomed.

food.name: Beef Shatkora
food.desc: Slow-cooked beef curry perfumed with shatkora, the bitter-fragrant Sylheti citrus. The dish every Sylheti household and restaurant is judged on.

places.name: Panshi Restaurant
places.note: The city institution for Sylheti home-style cooking; its shatkora beef is the local benchmark.

places.name: Pach Bhai Restaurant
places.note: Long-running rival to Panshi, singled out in guides for rice-and-shatkora-beef platters.

places.name: Palki Restaurant
places.note: Family-style Bengali dining room serving a milder, richer take on the citrus beef.

food.name: Shutki Bhorta
food.desc: Pungent dried-fish mash pounded with mustard oil, garlic and green chilli. Sylhet is the dried-fish capital of Bangladesh.

places.name: Panshi Restaurant
places.note: Lays out a whole counter of bhortas at lunch, with several shutki variations daily.

places.name: Pach Bhai Restaurant
places.note: Popular for the fiery chepa shutki bhorta eaten with plain rice.

places.name: Bhojon Bari
places.note: Everyday local canteen where bhorta thalis are the main draw.

food.name: Akhni Pulao
food.desc: Sylhet's own pilaf: short-grain rice cooked with beef or chicken and panch phoron style whole spices, lighter and tangier than biryani.

places.name: Panshi Restaurant
places.note: Serves akhni all day; the version most visitors are pointed to first.

places.name: Woondaal King Kebab
places.note: Kebab house whose akhni and beef tehari draw evening queues.

places.name: Palki Restaurant
places.note: Reliable akhni plus mutton rezala in a comfortable sit-down room.

food.name: Beef Kala Bhuna
food.desc: Beef reduced for hours with roasted spices until almost black and jammy. A Chittagong classic that Sylhet kitchens have made their own.

places.name: Woondaal King Kebab
places.note: Grill-focused kitchen known for deeply reduced kala bhuna and seekh kebabs.

places.name: Pach Bhai Restaurant
places.note: Kala bhuna with paratha is the standard order here at dinner.

places.name: Panshi Restaurant
places.note: Cooks it in daily batches; go early before the pot runs out.

food.name: Surma River Fish Curry
food.desc: Boal, ayre or chital from the Surma and haor wetlands simmered with panch phoron, tomato and coriander. Freshwater fish is the regional pride.

places.name: Panshi Restaurant
places.note: Fish counter changes with the catch; ask what came from the haor that morning.

places.name: Palki Restaurant
places.note: Good for larger fish steaks cooked to order for a table.

places.name: Lal Bazar Fish Market
places.note: The wholesale market itself, ringed by cook-your-catch stalls and the best place to see the haor fish.

food.name: Chunga Pitha and Sylheti Sweets
food.desc: Sticky rice steamed inside bamboo tubes, plus jaggery pithas and monda sweets sold from winter stalls and old confectioners.

places.name: Bandar Bazar stalls
places.note: Old bazaar lane where pitha vendors set up through the cool months.

places.name: Panshi Restaurant
places.note: Keeps seasonal pithas and traditional desserts on the menu alongside the mains.

places.name: Zindabazar street stalls
places.note: Evening carts frying pitha and selling monda a few steps from the main restaurants.

food.name: Seven-Layer Tea
food.desc: Sylhet's signature party trick: a glass of tea in seven distinct coloured bands that stay separated, invented in the surrounding tea district.

places.name: Nilkontho Tea Cabin
places.note: The original seven-colour tea cabin in the tea-garden town two hours from the city; the pilgrimage stop.

places.name: Ambarkhana tea cabins
places.note: City-centre cabins pouring five- and seven-layer glasses without the trip out of town.

places.name: Zindabazar tea stalls
places.note: Cheap street cabins for standard doodh cha and malai cha late into the night.

food.name: Lassi, Borhani and Sugarcane Juice
food.desc: Non-alcoholic staples: sweet or salted yoghurt lassi, spiced borhani drunk with rice dishes, and cane juice pressed at the roadside.

places.name: Bandar Bazar juice stalls
places.note: Rows of hand-cranked sugarcane presses and lassi churns in the old market.

places.name: Panshi Restaurant
places.note: Serves borhani by the jug, the traditional partner to akhni and kebabs.

places.name: Ambarkhana juice bars
places.note: Fresh lime, cane and green-coconut drinks near the busiest intersection.

landmarks: Shrine of Hazrat Shah Jalal
Bangladesh's most venerated Sufi shrine, the resting place of the 14th-century saint who brought Islam to Sylhet, thronged by pilgrims day and night.
Shrine of Hazrat Shah Paran
The serene hilltop mausoleum of Shah Jalal's nephew and fellow saint, shaded by an ancient sacred tree just east of the city.
Bichanakandi
A dazzling meeting point of rivers and stone beds at the Meghalaya foothills, where waterfalls tumble from India into ice-cold turquoise shallows.
Malnicherra Tea Estate
The subcontinent's oldest tea garden, planted in 1854, draping the hills at Sylhet's edge with photogenic emerald rows of tea bushes.
Keane Bridge and Surma riverfront
Sylhet's 1936 iron gateway across the Surma River, best viewed at dusk beside the Ali Amjad clock house and bustling ghats.
Ali Amjad's Clock Tower
A charming 1874 red-and-green clock house on the Surma's north bank, the city's oldest landmark and beloved meeting point.
Volaganj Sada Pathor
A surreal expanse of white stones scattered across the Dholai River at the border hills, glittering against clear water and green mountains.
Shahi Eidgah
A hilltop Mughal-era prayer ground built around 1700, its stepped white terraces gathering tens of thousands of worshippers for Eid prayers each year.
Osmani Museum
The former home of General M.A.G. Osmani, Bangladesh's independence war commander, displaying his uniform, medals, and personal effects in central Sylhet.
Museum of Rajas'
A folk museum in Zindabazar packed with traditional musical instruments, mystic poets' artifacts, and mementos of Sylhet's folk hero Hason Raja.

train.note: Domestic intercity trains (Parabat, Jayantika, Upaban, Kalni Express) run from Sylhet Railway Station to Dhaka and Chittagong; there are no cross-border passenger trains from Sylhet.

bus.note: There is no direct international coach. To reach India you take a local bus to the Tamabil border (about 55 km, ~2.5 hrs), cross on foot into Dawki in Meghalaya, then hire a shared taxi or jeep on to Shillong. Frequent domestic coaches (Green Line, Ena, Hanif) link Sylhet with Dhaka and Chittagong.

ferry.note: Sylhet is inland with no scheduled passenger ferry service, though seasonal country boats cross the Surma River and reach wetland sites like Ratargul during the monsoon.

half.name: Ratargul Swamp Forest
half.blurb: Bangladesh's only freshwater swamp forest, explored by country boat when flooded in the monsoon, about 26 km from the city.

half.name: Jaflong
half.blurb: Stone-strewn river valley under the Khasi hills at the Indian border, with tea gardens and the Dawki river, about 60 km northeast.

half.name: Bisnakandi
half.blurb: Where hill streams meet stacked boulders below the Meghalaya cliffs, a scenic clear-water spot near the border.

half.name: Lalakhal
half.blurb: A turquoise stretch of the Sari River framed by tea estates and forest, reached by wooden boat.

full.name: Sreemangal
full.blurb: Bangladesh's tea capital of rolling green estates, seven-layer tea and Lawachara rainforest, about 2.5 hrs southwest.

full.name: Lawachara National Park
full.blurb: Semi-evergreen rainforest near Sreemangal home to hoolock gibbons and rich birdlife.
